query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent, slow‐growing protective oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by the selective oxidation kinetics of the X element. When X is Al, its slower oxidation and the resulting formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 (possibly complemented by Cr2O3) scale reduce thermal mismatch and diffusional stress, whereas when X is Mn (or possibly Si), the faster, less controlled oxidation produces discontinuous or non-adherent oxide phases that tend to crack and spall.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state with near-equiatomic proportions.
generation.intervention: Exposing the alloy to high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation at approximately 950 °C in air (or a controlled oxygen partial pressure environment) for extended durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The nature (continuity, adhesion, growth rate) of the oxide scale formed—whether a slowly growing, continuous Al2O3-based layer forms versus a rapidly growing, cracked Mn- or Si-rich oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of the X element controls the oxide formation kinetics. In Al-containing alloys, the preferential, slow oxidation of Al yields a protective Al2O3 scale with better lattice matching and lower thermal expansion mismatch, enhancing adhesion and longevity. In contrast, Mn (or Si) promotes the rapid formation of oxides with higher diffusivity and less favorable mechanical properties, leading to spallation under thermal stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature oxidative conditions, Al-substituted HEAs will develop a slow-growing, continuous, and adherent oxide layer that remains intact over prolonged exposure, while Mn- or Si-substituted alloys will form oxide scales that crack or spall due to poor adherence and higher growth rates.
generation.baseline: A CrFeCoNi alloy variant with an inert or less reactive X element that does not significantly contribute to the formation of the protective oxide layer under similar high-temperature exposures.
generation.boundary: Test conditions are restricted to high-temperature (>900 °C) exposures in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres, over extended durations (e.g., 100 hours), and within the compositional range of near-equiatomic solid solutions achievable in these HEAs.
generation.uncertainty: The role of Si as the X element is less firmly established compared to Al and Mn, and additional factors such as microstructural features or slight compositional deviations may also influence oxide formation kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys where X is systematically varied among Al, Mn, and Si under identical fabrication conditions. Expose all samples to 950 °C in an air (or controlled oxygen) atmosphere for extended durations (e.g., 100 hours). Analyze the oxide scales using in situ high-temperature XRD, SEM cross-sectional imaging, and weight gain measurements.
measurements: Phase identification of the oxide scale via XRD
Characterization of oxide scale continuity and evidence of cracking/spallation via SEM
Oxidation kinetics determined by weight gain measurements
Thermal expansion mismatch assessments if possible
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing samples do not exhibit a more continuous, adherent, and slower-growing oxide scale than the Mn- or Si-containing samples, or if the Mn (or Si) variants also form a stable oxide more comparable to the Al case, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. ## Abstract
AbstractAs protective coatings for the thermal parts of aero-engines, AlCoCrFeNi coatings have good application prospects. In this study, atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) was used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy coatings (HECs), which were oxidized from 650 °C to 1000 °C. The mechanism of the oxide layer formation and the internal phase transition were systematically investigated. The results show that a mixed oxide scale with a laminated structure was formed at the initial stage of oxidation. The redistribution of elements and phase transition occurred in the HECs’ matrix; the BCC/B2 structure transformed to Al-Ni ordered B2 phase and Fe-Cr disordered A2 phase.Keywords: plasma spraying, oxidation behavior, high-entropy coatings, phase transition
